keyVerseText: And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew root טוּל (ṭûwl) is a primitive verb that fundamentally conveys the action of casting or throwing, often with force or intent to remove or displace. Its core sense involves the physical act of hurling or pitching something over or out, which extends metaphorically to sending away or casting down. This literal sense of forceful projection adds depth beyond the simple English gloss 'cast,' highlighting not just placement but active removal or rejection.
usageInScripture: Throughout its 14 occurrences, טוּל consistently carries the meaning of casting or throwing, whether literally as in the throwing of a javelin or figuratively in the sense of being cast down or sent away. The top translations, including 'cast,' 'will carry thee away,' and 'will cast thee out,' show a range that emphasizes both physical and metaphorical displacement. This consistency reveals the word’s role in describing decisive actions of removal or judgment.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding טוּל enriches our grasp of divine and human agency in Scripture where casting or throwing symbolizes judgment, protection, or conflict. It reflects the seriousness of God’s and man’s actions in removing opposition or danger, but also the vulnerability of those who are cast down. For the Christian faith, this word reminds us of Christ’s ultimate victory in bearing rejection and casting out sin, illustrating the power of God to decisively deal with evil while calling believers into a life of trust amid trials.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Samuel 18:11, 'And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it,' the word טוּל vividly conveys Saul’s aggressive intent to harm David by physically hurling a weapon. The use of this verb intensifies the scene, showing Saul’s violent determination and the real danger David faced. This highlights the human reality of conflict and God’s providential protection over David, who avoided Saul’s deadly cast twice.
